title: Oatmeal for a Hangover: Does It Help? Slow Carbs, Explained
excerpt: Is oatmeal good for a hangover? How slow carbs help low blood sugar and a queasy stomach, which oats to pick, why eating oats before drinking matters, and what oatmeal can't fix.
metaDescription: Is oatmeal good for a hangover? How slow carbs steady blood sugar, ease a queasy stomach, which oats are best, and why eating before drinking matters most.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** oatmeal is one of the better things you can eat the morning after drinking, but it isn't a hangover cure. It gives you slow, steady carbohydrates when your blood sugar may be running low, it's gentle on a queasy stomach, it carries water into your body, and it brings along some of the minerals and B vitamins that drinking can use up. What it can't do is clear alcohol faster, undo the inflammation behind a hangover, or fix a pounding headache on its own. Think of it as a smart, easy breakfast that helps you feel more human, not as a remedy.

**The quick version of what to do:** make a bowl of plain rolled or steel-cut oats with water or milk, add a banana or some berries, a pinch of salt, and a spoonful of nut butter or a side of eggs for protein. Drink a big glass of water with it. If your stomach is rough, start with a few spoonfuls and wait ten minutes. And if you're planning ahead, a bowl of oatmeal *before* you go out is arguably more useful than one after, because food in your stomach slows how fast alcohol reaches your blood.

> **When to see a doctor.** A hangover is miserable but it passes on its own, usually within a day. Get medical help if you can't keep any fluids down for more than several hours, you're vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds, you have severe stomach pain that won't settle, you're confused, very drowsy, or hard to wake, your breathing is slow or irregular, or you have a seizure. Those are not hangover symptoms; they can point to alcohol poisoning, dangerous dehydration, or a problem like pancreatitis. Call 911 (or your local emergency number) for anyone who can't be woken or is breathing strangely. If you shake, sweat, or feel very anxious every time you stop drinking, that's worth raising with a doctor too, because it can be a sign of alcohol withdrawal rather than an ordinary hangover. You can read more in our guide to [alcohol poisoning signs](/never-hungover/alcohol-poisoning-signs).

## Is Oatmeal Good for a Hangover?

Yes, as a breakfast choice it's a good one. The case for oatmeal rests on four ordinary things, none of which are magic:

1. **It's slow-release carbohydrate.** Oats break down gradually, so they give your body a steady supply of glucose rather than a quick spike and crash.
2. **It's bland and soft.** When you're nauseous, plain, warm, low-fat food tends to sit better than anything greasy, spicy, or acidic.
3. **It's mostly water once cooked.** A bowl of oatmeal made with water or milk is a surprisingly hydrating meal, which matters when you're short on fluids.
4. **It carries useful nutrients.** Oats contain magnesium, zinc, iron, and B vitamins such as thiamine, plus a type of soluble fiber called beta-glucan.

Here's the important caveat. There's no good evidence that oatmeal, or any single food, shortens a hangover or makes it less severe. Researchers who study hangovers have looked at all sorts of foods and supplements, and so far nothing eaten the morning after has been shown in solid trials to reliably cure one. Oatmeal earns its place because it addresses a few of the things that make you feel worse (low energy, an empty stomach, too little fluid) while being easy to get down. That's a modest claim, but it's an honest one.

## Why You Feel So Bad: What a Hangover Actually Is

It helps to know what you're up against, because it explains what food can and can't do.

A hangover is a bundle of overlapping problems, and scientists still argue about which ones matter most. The main suspects are:

- **Acetaldehyde.** When your liver breaks down alcohol, the first by-product is acetaldehyde, a toxic compound that's normally cleared quickly. When you drink a lot, it can build up and contribute to nausea, flushing, and a racing heart.
- **Inflammation.** Heavy drinking triggers an immune response. Higher levels of inflammatory signaling molecules have been linked with worse hangover symptoms, and many researchers now see inflammation as a central piece of the puzzle.
- **Poor sleep.** Alcohol may help you fall asleep, but it fragments sleep in the second half of the night. A lot of next-day fog is simply bad sleep.
- **Fluid loss.** Alcohol suppresses a hormone (vasopressin) that tells your kidneys to hold on to water, so you pee more. That's why you wake up thirsty with a dry mouth. Interestingly, studies haven't found that dehydration alone explains how bad a hangover feels, but it certainly doesn't help. See our piece on [whether alcohol really dehydrates you](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-dehydrate-you).
- **Stomach irritation.** Alcohol irritates the stomach lining and increases acid, which is behind a lot of the queasiness.
- **Low blood sugar.** Your liver normally keeps your blood sugar steady between meals. While it's busy processing alcohol, it's worse at that job, so blood sugar can dip, especially if you didn't eat much.

Oatmeal can help with the last few items on that list: an irritated stomach, low fluids, and low blood sugar. It does very little about acetaldehyde, inflammation, or the sleep you lost. That's the realistic frame for everything below.

## The Blood Sugar Angle: Why Slow Carbs Make Sense

The best argument for oatmeal is about energy.

Your liver has two jobs that clash after a night out. One is processing alcohol. The other is making new glucose to keep your blood sugar steady when you haven't eaten (a process called gluconeogenesis). Breaking down alcohol shifts the liver's chemistry in a way that slows that glucose production. If you drank on a light stomach, skipped dinner, or danced for hours, your blood sugar can be lower than usual the next morning.

Low blood sugar can make you feel shaky, weak, irritable, sweaty, and foggy, which overlaps a lot with how a hangover feels. To be fair to the evidence, research hasn't shown that low blood sugar is the main driver of hangover severity. Some studies have found only a weak link between blood sugar and how bad people feel. But for many people, eating something with carbohydrate is one of the quickest ways to feel a bit steadier.

This is where oats shine compared with, say, a can of soda or a pastry:

- **Fiber slows digestion.** The soluble fiber in oats (beta-glucan) forms a gel in the gut that slows how quickly sugar reaches your blood. That gives you a gentler rise and a longer, steadier supply of energy.
- **Less of a crash.** A sugary breakfast can give a quick lift followed by a dip a couple of hours later, which is the last thing you need when you already feel rough.
- **Room to add protein.** Oatmeal pairs easily with milk, yogurt, nut butter, or eggs, and protein slows digestion further.

If you want quick sugar, there's a place for it too, especially if you feel faint and shaky. A glass of juice or a sports drink can work fast, and then oatmeal can keep you going afterward. Our guide to [sugar for a hangover](/never-hungover/sugar-for-hangover) covers when fast sugar helps and when it backfires.

## Steel-Cut, Rolled, or Instant: Which Oats Are Best?

All oats start as the same whole grain. The difference is how much they've been cut, steamed, and flattened, which changes how fast they cook and how quickly they raise your blood sugar.

| Type | How it's made | Cooking time | Blood sugar effect | Best for a hangover when... |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Steel-cut oats | Whole oat kernels chopped into pieces | About 20 to 30 minutes on the stove | Slowest, steadiest rise | You made them ahead or have the patience to wait |
| Rolled (old-fashioned) oats | Steamed and flattened into flakes | About 5 minutes on the stove, 2 to 3 in the microwave | Moderate, steady rise | You want a good balance of speed and slow energy (the best all-round pick) |
| Quick oats | Rolled thinner and cut smaller | 1 to 2 minutes | Faster rise | You need food very quickly |
| Instant packets | Pre-cooked, dried, often sweetened and flavored | Add hot water | Fastest rise, especially flavored ones with added sugar | You have nothing else; choose plain where possible |

**Our pick for a hangover morning: plain rolled oats.** They're quick enough to make when you feel terrible, they keep much of the slow-energy benefit, and they're easy on the stomach. If you have flavored instant packets, they're still better than skipping breakfast, but check the label. Many contain a fair amount of added sugar, which works against the steady-energy idea.

## Oatmeal and an Upset Stomach

Nausea is one of the most common hangover complaints, and it's often what stops people from eating at all. Oatmeal is a good first food for a sensitive stomach for a few reasons:

- **It's low in fat.** Fatty food stays in the stomach longer, and greasy breakfasts can make nausea worse for some people. Plain oatmeal is very low in fat.
- **It's soft and warm.** Warm, soft foods tend to be easier to get down than anything crunchy, cold, or strongly flavored.
- **It's not acidic or spicy.** Alcohol already irritates the stomach lining. Oatmeal won't add to that the way orange juice, coffee on an empty stomach, or hot sauce might.
- **You control the dose.** You can eat three spoonfuls, pause, and see how you feel.

**How to eat it when you feel sick:**

1. Sip some water first and wait a few minutes. If that stays down, you're ready for food.
2. Make a small, thin bowl, cooked with extra water so it's softer and easier to swallow.
3. Keep it plain. Skip the chocolate, heavy cream, and big dollops of peanut butter for now.
4. Eat slowly, a few spoonfuls at a time.
5. If plain oatmeal is still too much, try dry toast or crackers first, then come back to oatmeal later. Our guide to [toast and crackers for a hangover](/never-hungover/toast-and-crackers-for-hangover) explains why those bland carbs work.

A little grated ginger stirred into your oatmeal is a reasonable addition if you're queasy. Ginger has some evidence for easing nausea in other settings, though it hasn't been well studied for hangovers specifically. For more help, see our full guide to [hangover nausea and stomach relief](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025).

## The Nutrients in Oats, and Why They Matter After Drinking

Oats are more nutritious than they look. A typical serving of half a cup of dry rolled oats has roughly 150 calories, about 27 grams of carbohydrate, around 4 grams of fiber, and around 5 grams of protein, along with useful amounts of several minerals. Exact numbers vary by brand, so check your packet.

Here's how the main nutrients line up with what drinking does to your body:

- **Magnesium.** Alcohol increases how much magnesium you lose through urine. Oats are a decent source. A single bowl won't correct a deficiency, but it contributes.
- **B vitamins, especially thiamine (B1).** Heavy, long-term drinking can deplete thiamine, which the body needs to turn food into energy. Oats provide some thiamine. For an occasional night out, this matters less than it does for regular heavy drinkers.
- **Zinc.** Zinc is involved in the enzymes that break down alcohol. Oats contain a meaningful amount. One small study has suggested people with more zinc in their diets reported somewhat milder hangovers, but that's early observational evidence, not proof.
- **Potassium.** Oats contain some potassium, and adding a banana boosts it. The idea that a hangover is caused by low potassium is mostly a myth for ordinary drinking, but a banana is still a good, gentle food. Our article on [bananas for a hangover](/never-hungover/bananas-for-hangover) digs into that.
- **Beta-glucan.** This soluble fiber is what gives oats their slow-energy effect. It's also the reason the FDA allows oat products to carry a claim about heart health, based on its ability to lower cholesterol over time. That's a long-term benefit rather than a hangover one, but it's a nice bonus.

The realistic takeaway is that oatmeal helps restock some of what drinking draws down, in a form your stomach can handle. It isn't a fast fix for a mineral deficiency, and it doesn't detox anything.

## Oatmeal Before Drinking: The More Useful Move

If you're reading this before a night out, here's the most practical advice on the page: **eat a proper meal before you drink, and oatmeal is a fine choice.**

Food in your stomach slows down how quickly alcohol passes into your small intestine, which is where most of it is absorbed. That means your blood alcohol rises more slowly and peaks lower than it would on an empty stomach. This is well established, and it's one of the few pre-drinking habits with solid evidence behind it. A lower, slower peak tends to mean you feel less drunk, make better choices about the next drink, and may feel less awful the following day.

Oatmeal works well as a pre-drinking meal because its fiber and slow digestion keep food in your stomach for a while. It works even better with some protein and fat alongside it, since a mixed meal slows things down more than carbohydrate alone. A bowl of oats with milk, nuts, and fruit a couple of hours before you go out, or a hearty dinner with a side of oats, is a solid base.

One thing to be clear about: eating first lowers your peak blood alcohol, but it doesn't change how much alcohol you've drunk. Your liver still has to process every drink at its usual pace of roughly one standard drink per hour. Food buys you a gentler ride, not a free pass. For more on why skipping food before drinking is a bad bet, see [drinking on an empty stomach](/never-hungover/drinking-on-an-empty-stomach).

## Overnight Oats: The Hangover Breakfast You Make the Night Before

If you know you're going out, the smartest thing you can do for future-you is make overnight oats before you leave. When you wake up feeling rough, breakfast is already waiting in the fridge, and there's nothing to cook.

**Basic overnight oats (one serving):**

- Half a cup of rolled oats
- Half to three-quarters of a cup of milk or a milk alternative
- A few spoonfuls of plain yogurt (optional, for protein and creaminess)
- A pinch of salt
- Half a sliced banana or a handful of berries
- A teaspoon of honey or maple syrup if you like it sweeter

Stir everything together in a jar, cover it, and put it in the fridge. By morning, the oats have softened into a thick, pudding-like texture. You can eat it cold, which some people find easier when nauseous, or warm it in the microwave for a minute.

A cold breakfast can actually be easier to tolerate for some people with a hangover, because strong smells from hot food can trigger nausea. If hot food turns your stomach, overnight oats are a good workaround.

## How to Build a Better Hangover Bowl

Plain oatmeal is a good start. A few additions make it better without making it hard on your stomach.

**Base:** half a cup of rolled oats cooked in water or milk. Milk adds protein and fluid. Water is gentler if dairy doesn't agree with you that morning.

**Add some salt.** A small pinch of salt does more than improve flavor. You lose sodium through extra urination, and a little salt helps your body hold on to the water you're drinking. It's a small, sensible addition, not a treatment.

**Add fruit:**

- **Banana:** soft, easy on the stomach, adds potassium and natural sweetness.
- **Berries:** add flavor, fiber, and plant antioxidants.
- **Applesauce:** a gentle, bland option if your stomach is very sensitive.

**Add protein (once your stomach is settled):**

- A spoonful of peanut or almond butter
- A dollop of Greek yogurt
- A side of eggs. Eggs contain an amino acid called cysteine, which is involved in clearing acetaldehyde; whether eating eggs helps with that in practice is unproven, but they're a good protein source. More in our article on [eggs for a hangover](/never-hungover/eggs-for-hangover).

**Add a little sweetness if you want it:** a drizzle of honey or maple syrup is fine. There's no need to avoid sugar entirely; just keep it modest so the oats stay a slow-energy meal.

**Add ginger if you're queasy:** a little fresh grated ginger or a pinch of ground ginger.

**Drink alongside it:** a big glass of water, or an electrolyte drink if you've been vomiting. Our guide on [whether water helps a hangover](/never-hungover/does-water-help-a-hangover) covers how much to drink and when plain water is enough.

For more ideas, see our [best hangover breakfast recipes](/never-hungover/best-hangover-breakfast) and our broader list of the [best foods for a hangover](/never-hungover/best-foods-for-hangover).

## Oatmeal vs Other Hangover Breakfasts

How does a bowl of oats compare with the other things people reach for?

| Breakfast | What it does well | Drawbacks after drinking |
|---|---|---|
| Oatmeal | Slow energy, gentle on the stomach, hydrating, easy to add protein and fruit | Not filling on its own without protein; plain can taste dull |
| Toast or crackers | Very bland, fast, good first food when nauseous | Little protein or fiber, energy fades quickly |
| Eggs | Protein, keeps you full, easy to digest | Fried versions can be heavy; some people can't face them when queasy |
| Greasy fry-up or fast food | Satisfying, salty | High fat can worsen nausea and heartburn; doesn't speed recovery |
| Pastries or sugary cereal | Quick sugar hit | Fast rise and drop in energy; little else nutritionally |
| Soup or broth | Fluid and salt, very gentle | Low in energy unless it has noodles, rice, or meat |
| Nothing at all | Nothing | Blood sugar stays low, you feel weaker, and painkillers are harder on an empty stomach |

The best realistic approach for most people is a combination: oatmeal for steady energy, something with protein, and plenty of fluid. You don't need a perfect meal. Eating something reasonable is far better than eating nothing.

## Common Myths About Oatmeal and Hangovers

**"Oatmeal absorbs the alcohol."** It doesn't. Food eaten before drinking slows how fast alcohol is absorbed, but it doesn't soak alcohol up like a sponge, and eating oatmeal the next morning does nothing to alcohol that's already been absorbed. By the time you wake up, most of it has usually been processed anyway.

**"Oats detox your liver."** There's no good evidence that oatmeal speeds up how your liver clears alcohol or its by-products. Your liver works through alcohol at a fairly fixed pace, and no breakfast changes that.

**"The fiber sweeps toxins out of your body."** Fiber is good for digestion and blood sugar, but it doesn't remove acetaldehyde or other hangover-related compounds from your bloodstream.

**"Oat milk is just as good."** Oat milk is a fine drink, but it's mostly water with a small amount of oats, and many brands have added oils and sugar. It doesn't carry the fiber or slow-energy benefits of a bowl of actual oats. It's a reasonable liquid to cook your oats in, though.

**"Instant oatmeal is useless."** Not true. Plain instant oats are still oats. They raise blood sugar a bit faster than rolled or steel-cut, and flavored packets often have added sugar, but if instant is what you have, it's still a good breakfast.

## Who Should Be Careful With Oatmeal

Oatmeal is safe for nearly everyone, but a few groups should pay attention:

- **People with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.** Oats are naturally gluten-free, but they're often grown and processed alongside wheat, barley, and rye, so regular oats can be contaminated. Look for oats labeled gluten-free. A small number of people with celiac disease also react to a protein in oats themselves, so check with your doctor if you're unsure.
- **People with diabetes.** Alcohol can cause low blood sugar in people taking insulin or certain diabetes medicines, sometimes many hours after drinking. Oatmeal can be part of a sensible breakfast, but follow your own care plan and check your levels. Our guide on [alcohol and blood sugar management](/never-hungover/alcohol-diabetes-blood-sugar-management-guide-2025) covers this in more detail.
- **Anyone with a sensitive gut.** A large bowl of high-fiber food can cause bloating or gas in some people, especially if your gut is already upset. Start with a smaller portion.

## What Oatmeal Won't Fix

It's worth being direct about the limits:

- **It won't cure the headache.** If you need pain relief, think carefully about which one. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) and alcohol can be a risky mix for the liver, and ibuprofen can irritate a stomach that's already sore, so eat first and follow the label.
- **It won't replace sleep.** Much of the hangover fog is lost sleep, and the best fix is rest when you can get it.
- **It won't rehydrate you on its own.** It helps, but you still need to drink fluids through the day.
- **It won't make the next night of drinking safer.** The most reliable ways to have fewer hangovers are drinking less, drinking more slowly, alternating with water, and eating before and while you drink. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) goes through what has the best evidence.

## Where Supplements Fit In

Some people pair good habits like eating before drinking with a supplement. The one we write about most is **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a compound from the Japanese raisin tree. Animal and lab studies suggest it may influence how the body handles alcohol and acetaldehyde, and there's a small amount of human research, but the human evidence is limited and it isn't a guaranteed fix. It also doesn't replace food, water, or sleep, and it doesn't make heavy drinking safe.

If you want to try it as one piece of a sensible routine, two widely used options are [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the lower-cost [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much people typically take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands honestly. Check with a doctor or pharmacist first if you take regular medication.

## The Bottom Line

- Oatmeal is a good hangover breakfast, but there's no good evidence that it, or any single food, cures a hangover.
- Its real benefits are slow, steady energy for low blood sugar, a gentle option for a queasy stomach, extra fluid, and some of the minerals and B vitamins drinking can use up.
- Plain rolled oats are the best all-round pick: quick to make, easy on the stomach, and slow to digest. Watch the added sugar in flavored instant packets.
- Add a banana or berries, a pinch of salt, and some protein once your stomach settles, and drink water with it.
- Eating oatmeal, or any real meal, *before* drinking is even more useful, because food slows how quickly alcohol reaches your blood.
- Overnight oats made before you go out mean breakfast is ready when you least feel like cooking.
- See a doctor if you can't keep fluids down, have severe stomach pain, are vomiting blood, or are confused or hard to wake.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is oatmeal good for a hangover?**

Yes, as a breakfast it's one of the better choices. It provides slow-release carbohydrate that can help if your blood sugar is low, it's bland and easy on a queasy stomach, it adds fluid, and it contains magnesium, zinc, and B vitamins. There's no good evidence that it cures a hangover or makes it end sooner, but it can help you feel steadier while your body recovers.

**Should I eat oatmeal before drinking?**

Eating a proper meal before drinking is one of the most useful things you can do, and oatmeal is a good option. Food in your stomach slows how quickly alcohol is absorbed, so your blood alcohol rises more slowly and peaks lower. Oatmeal works even better with some protein and fat, such as milk, nuts, or eggs. It doesn't change how much alcohol your liver has to process, though, so pacing yourself still matters.

**What kind of oatmeal is best for a hangover?**

Plain rolled (old-fashioned) oats are the best all-round pick. They cook in a few minutes, they're gentle on the stomach, and they release energy slowly. Steel-cut oats are even slower to digest but take longer to make, so they're ideal if you prepared them ahead. Instant oats are fine too; just choose plain versions where you can, since flavored packets often contain a lot of added sugar.

**Can oatmeal help with hangover nausea?**

It can be one of the easier foods to keep down when you're queasy, because it's soft, warm, low in fat, and not acidic. Start with a small, thin bowl, keep it plain, and eat slowly. A little grated ginger can be a reasonable addition. If even oatmeal is too much, try dry toast or crackers first. If you can't keep fluids down for more than several hours, see a doctor.

**Are overnight oats good for a hangover?**

Yes. They're the same nutrition as cooked oats, and making them the night before means breakfast is ready when you don't feel like cooking. Some people also find a cold breakfast easier to face when nauseous, because hot food smells can make queasiness worse. Mix rolled oats with milk or yogurt, a pinch of salt, and some fruit, and leave the jar in the fridge overnight.

**Does oatmeal absorb alcohol?**

No. Eating before you drink slows how fast alcohol gets into your blood, but oatmeal doesn't soak up alcohol like a sponge, and eating it the next morning does nothing to alcohol that's already been absorbed. Your liver still processes alcohol at its usual pace, roughly one standard drink per hour.

**What should I put in my oatmeal when I'm hungover?**

Good additions include a sliced banana or berries for flavor and potassium, a pinch of salt to help your body hold on to fluids, and a source of protein such as Greek yogurt, nut butter, or a side of eggs once your stomach settles. A small drizzle of honey is fine. Keep it simple and low in fat if you're nauseous, and drink a big glass of water with it.

**Is oat milk good for a hangover?**

Oat milk is a fine drink and a reasonable liquid to cook oatmeal in, but on its own it doesn't offer the same benefits as a bowl of oats. It's mostly water with a small amount of oats, it has little fiber, and many brands contain added oil and sugar. For hydration, water or an electrolyte drink is a better choice.
